questionText: Which sentence uses ABSTRACT as a verb (ab-STRACT)?
options: A) She was able to abstract key data from the lengthy report.
B) The painting was completely abstract, with no recognisable shapes.
C) He presented an abstract of his research to the committee.
D) The abstract art exhibition drew large crowds.
explanation: ABSTRACT as a verb (ab-STRACT) means to extract or summarise information. As a noun (AB-stract) it means a summary. As an adjective (AB-stract) it means not concrete. The verb is stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: Which sentence uses ATTRIBUTE as a verb (at-TRIB-ute)?
options: A) Critics attribute the painting to a student of Rembrandt.
B) Her patience is her greatest attribute.
C) His main attribute was his extraordinary memory.
D) The attribute of honesty is highly valued.
explanation: ATTRIBUTE as a verb (at-TRIB-ute) means to regard something as caused by. As a noun (AT-trib-ute), stressed on the first syllable, it means a characteristic or quality.

questionText: Which sentence uses CONTENT as an adjective (con-TENT)?
options: A) She was content to sit quietly and read her book.
B) The content of the report was reviewed by experts.
C) The website content was updated daily.
D) The minister reviewed the content of the new policy.
explanation: CONTENT as an adjective (con-TENT, stressed on the second syllable) means satisfied. As a noun (CON-tent, first syllable stress) it means the material inside something or a subject.

questionText: The word WOUND is a homograph. What are its two meanings?
options: A) An injury (past tense of WIND as in coiled) OR past tense of WIND (to turn)
B) An injury OR past tense of HURT
C) Past tense of WIND (to coil) OR a hole in the ground
D) An injury OR a musical note
explanation: WOUND has two meanings: 1) a wound /wuːnd/ meaning an injury to the body; 2) wound /waʊnd/ meaning the past tense of WIND (to coil or wrap), as in she wound the thread around the bobbin.

questionText: Which sentence uses SUBJECT as a verb (sub-JECT)?
options: A) The prisoners were subjected to harsh conditions.
B) History was his favourite subject at school.
C) The subject of the painting was a rural landscape.
D) All subjects were asked to sign a consent form.
explanation: SUBJECT as a verb (sub-JECT) means to cause someone to undergo something. As a noun or adjective (SUB-ject), stressed on the first syllable, it means a topic or a person under authority.

questionText: Which sentence uses REBEL as a noun (REB-el)?
options: A) The rebel refused to comply with any of the directives.
B) She would rebel against any authority she deemed unjust.
C) He decided to rebel against the school uniform policy.
D) Students sometimes rebel against strict rules.
explanation: REBEL as a noun (REB-el) means a person who resists authority, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (re-BEL) meaning to resist, it is stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: The word TEAR is a homograph. Which sentence uses TEAR meaning a drop of water from the eye?
options: A) A tear ran down her cheek as she read the letter.
B) He watched her tear the letter into tiny pieces.
C) Do not tear the pages when you turn them.
D) The dog managed to tear the cushion completely.
explanation: TEAR /tɪər/ means a drop of water from the eye when crying. TEAR /teər/ means to pull apart. A TEAR ran down her cheek uses the /tɪər/ pronunciation.

questionText: Which sentence uses OBJECT as a verb (ob-JECT)?
options: A) Several members objected to the proposed changes.
B) The glass object on the shelf was very old.
C) The object of the exercise was to improve teamwork.
D) She picked up a small object from the floor.
explanation: OBJECT as a verb (ob-JECT) means to express disagreement or disapproval. As a noun (OB-ject), stressed on the first syllable, it means a physical thing or purpose.

questionText: The word MINUTE is a heteronym. Which sentence uses it as an adjective meaning extremely small?
options: A) The scientists found minute traces of the chemical compound.
B) Please wait a minute while I check the information.
C) The meeting lasted exactly sixty minutes.
D) I will be there in one minute.
explanation: MINUTE as an adjective (my-NEWT) means extremely small, stressed on the second syllable. As a noun (MIN-it) meaning 60 seconds, it is stressed on the first syllable.

questionText: Which sentence uses INCLINE as a noun (IN-cline)?
options: A) The cyclists struggled up the steep incline.
B) I am inclined to agree with your assessment.
C) She did not incline toward either of the options.
D) His head inclined slightly as he listened.
explanation: INCLINE as a noun (IN-cline) means a slope or gradient, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (in-CLINE) meaning to lean or tend toward, it is stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: The word ROW is a homograph. What are its two meanings?
options: A) A line of things OR to propel a boat with oars OR a noisy argument
B) A line of things OR a type of dance
C) To propel a boat OR a type of singing
D) A noisy argument OR to plant seeds
explanation: ROW has multiple meanings: 1) /rəʊ/ a line of things arranged side by side; 2) /rəʊ/ to propel a boat using oars; 3) /raʊ/ British English for a noisy argument. Options 1 and 2 are homophones; option 3 has a different pronunciation.

questionText: Which sentence uses EXCERPT as a verb (ex-CERPT)?
options: A) The editor excerpted several passages from the original novel.
B) She read an excerpt from the novel to the audience.
C) The excerpt chosen was from the third chapter.
D) He shared a brief excerpt from his unpublished manuscript.
explanation: EXCERPT as a verb (ex-CERPT) means to take a passage from a larger work. As a noun (EX-cerpt), stressed on the first syllable, it means a short passage taken from a book or other text.

questionText: Which sentence uses CONFLICT as a verb (con-FLICT)?
options: A) The witness testimony conflicted with the official account.
B) The conflict between the two nations lasted three years.
C) The internal conflict tore the organisation apart.
D) Every conflict has at least two sides.
explanation: CONFLICT as a verb (con-FLICT) means to be incompatible or at variance, stressed on the second syllable. As a noun (CON-flict) meaning a serious disagreement, it is stressed on the first syllable.

questionText: The word LEAD is a homograph. Which sentence uses LEAD meaning the metal?
options: A) The pipes in the old house were made of lead.
B) She decided to lead the team through the challenging project.
C) He took the lead in the race from the very start.
D) The politician was expected to lead the new coalition.
explanation: LEAD /lɛd/ is a heavy metal. LEAD /liːd/ means to guide or to be ahead. The pipes made of LEAD uses the metal meaning with the /lɛd/ pronunciation.

questionText: Which sentence uses PRODUCE as a noun (PRO-duce)?
options: A) The market sells fresh produce from local farms.
B) The factory aims to produce one thousand units daily.
C) Scientists can now produce new materials in the laboratory.
D) Modern methods can produce results more quickly.
explanation: PRODUCE as a noun (PRO-duce) refers to fresh fruit and vegetables, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (pro-DUCE) meaning to make or create, it is stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: Which sentence uses COORDINATE as a noun (co-OR-di-nate)?
options: A) Plot the coordinates on the graph carefully.
B) They need to coordinate their efforts for maximum impact.
C) Please coordinate with your team before proceeding.
D) We must coordinate the arrival times carefully.
explanation: COORDINATE as a noun (co-OR-di-nate or CO-or-di-nate) refers to a set of values defining a position. As a verb it means to organise activities efficiently.

questionText: The word BASS is a homograph. What are its two different pronunciations and meanings?
options: A) /beis/ a deep voice or musical pitch; /baes/ a type of fish
B) /beis/ and /baes/ both meaning a low musical note
C) /baes/ a fish and /baes/ a low musical note
D) /beis/ a musical term and /beis/ a type of wood
explanation: BASS /beɪs/ means a low voice or low frequency in music. BASS /baes/ means a type of freshwater fish. The identical spellings with different pronunciations and meanings make it a classic homograph.

questionText: Which sentence uses PERMIT as a noun (PER-mit)?
options: A) You will need a permit to park in this restricted area.
B) The rules do not permit smoking inside the building.
C) Will you permit me to explain the situation?
D) The authority does not permit access without identification.
explanation: PERMIT as a noun (PER-mit) means an official document granting permission, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (per-MIT) meaning to allow, it is stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: Which sentence uses PROTEST as a verb (pro-TEST)?
options: A) She protested vigorously against the unfair decision.
B) The protest outside parliament lasted three days.
C) The student joined the protest on campus.
D) The peaceful protest drew thousands of participants.
explanation: PROTEST as a verb (pro-TEST) means to express strong objection, stressed on the second syllable. As a noun (PRO-test) meaning a statement of objection, it is stressed on the first syllable.

questionText: The word WIND is a heteronym. Which sentence uses it as a verb meaning to coil or turn?
options: A) She began to wind the wool carefully into a ball.
B) The strong wind knocked over the trees along the street.
C) The wind from the north brought cold temperatures.
D) He shielded his face from the biting wind.
explanation: WIND as a verb /waɪnd/ means to turn or coil something around. WIND as a noun /wɪnd/ refers to moving air. She began to WIND the wool uses the verb pronunciation /waɪnd/.

questionText: Which sentence uses FREQUENT as a verb (fre-QUENT)?
options: A) He frequents the library almost every evening.
B) The area experiences frequent power outages.
C) She made frequent visits to the museum.
D) Frequent rainfall is common in this region.
explanation: FREQUENT as a verb (fre-QUENT) means to visit a place often, stressed on the second syllable. As an adjective (FRE-quent) meaning occurring often, it is stressed on the first syllable.

questionText: The word MOPED is a heteronym. What are its two uses?
options: A) A moped /moh-ped/ is a motorbike; moped /mohpt/ is past tense of mope
B) Both are pronounced the same and mean different things
C) A moped is a bike and is also past tense of map
D) Moped relates only to transportation
explanation: MOPED as a noun /ˈmoʊpɛd/ is a low-powered motorbike. MOPED as a past tense /moʊpt/ is the past tense of MOPE (to be unhappy and listless). The different pronunciations make them heteronyms.

questionText: Which sentence uses SUPPLEMENT as a verb (sup-ple-MENT)?
options: A) She supplemented her income with freelance writing.
B) The vitamin supplement helped improve her health.
C) The dietary supplement was recommended by the doctor.
D) He took a mineral supplement with breakfast each day.
explanation: SUPPLEMENT as a verb (sup-ple-MENT) means to add to something to improve it, stressed on the third syllable. As a noun (SUP-ple-ment) it means an additional substance or publication.

questionText: The word CLEAVE is a special homograph. What makes it unusual?
options: A) It has two opposite meanings: to split apart AND to cling to
B) It is only used in archaic English
C) It is both a noun and verb with the same pronunciation
D) It has the same meaning in all contexts
explanation: CLEAVE is a CONTRANYM (auto-antonym): it means both TO SPLIT APART (cleave wood with an axe) and TO CLING TO (she cleaved to her beliefs). Words with opposite meanings are called contranyms or Janus words.

questionText: Which sentence uses COMPLEX as a noun meaning a group of buildings?
options: A) The sports complex includes an Olympic-sized swimming pool.
B) His complex reasoning baffled the audience.
C) The complex equation took hours to solve.
D) She had a complex relationship with her family.
explanation: COMPLEX as a noun (COM-plex) refers to a group of related buildings or a psychological problem, stressed on the first syllable. As an adjective (com-PLEX or COM-plex) it means complicated.

questionText: Which sentence uses DUPLICATE as a verb (du-pli-CATE)?
options: A) The researchers were unable to duplicate the original results.
B) Please make a duplicate of this document for the records.
C) Keep the duplicate for your own reference.
D) A duplicate key was made in case of emergencies.
explanation: DUPLICATE as a verb (du-pli-CATE) means to make an exact copy or reproduce something. As a noun or adjective (DU-pli-cate) it means a copy or identical to another.

questionText: The word SEWER is a heteronym. What are its two meanings?
options: A) SEW-er (one who sews) OR SOO-er (a drain for waste water)
B) Both meanings relate to underground pipes
C) A sewer is only a drain and has one pronunciation
D) SEW-er means a drain and SOO-er means one who sews
explanation: SEWER has two meanings: /ˈsoʊər/ (rhymes with tower) means one who sews; /ˈsuːər/ means an underground pipe for carrying away waste water. Different pronunciations make these heteronyms.

questionText: Which sentence uses IMPACT as a verb (im-PACT)?
options: A) Rising costs are beginning to impact small businesses severely.
B) The impact of the collision was felt throughout the building.
C) The economic impact lasted several years.
D) The full impact of the storm was only visible the next morning.
explanation: IMPACT as a verb (im-PACT) means to have a strong effect on something. Note: some usage guides prefer affect or effect as verbs; however, im-PACT as a verb is widely accepted in modern English.

questionText: The word PRIMER is a heteronym. What are its two meanings?
options: A) PRIM-er (a first coat of paint) OR PRY-mer (an introductory book)
B) Both mean an introductory guide in all contexts
C) PRIM-er means a book and PRY-mer means paint
D) Both pronunciations mean the same thing
explanation: PRIMER as /ˈprɪmər/ means a first coat of paint or a preparatory substance. As /ˈpraɪmər/ (British) it means an elementary textbook. The two pronunciations distinguish the contexts.

questionText: Which sentence uses ALTERNATE as an adjective (al-TER-nate)?
options: A) She attends the meetings on alternate Fridays.
B) We need to find an alternate solution to the problem.
C) The plan was to alternate between two approaches.
D) They alternate leadership responsibilities every month.
explanation: ALTERNATE as an adjective (AL-ter-nate) means occurring by turns; every other one, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (al-TER-nate) it means to go back and forth between two things.

questionText: The word POLISH is a heteronym. What are its two meanings?
options: A) POL-ish (to make shiny) OR POL-ish (relating to Poland)
B) Both mean to clean something
C) POL-ish means relating to Poland and pol-ISH means to shine
D) The word has only one meaning and pronunciation
explanation: POLISH /ˈpɒlɪʃ/ (lowercase) means to make something smooth and shiny, or a substance used to do this. POLISH /ˈpoʊlɪʃ/ (capitalised) means relating to Poland. Words that change meaning based on capitalisation are CAPITONYMS.

questionText: Which sentence uses ADVOCATE as a verb (ad-vo-CATE)?
options: A) She strongly advocates for stricter environmental regulations.
B) The advocate presented a compelling case in court.
C) The patients advocate fought for better treatment.
D) He worked as an advocate for human rights organisations.
explanation: ADVOCATE as a verb (ad-vo-CATE) means to publicly recommend or support, stressed on the third syllable. As a noun (AD-vo-cate) it means a person who publicly supports a cause or a lawyer.

questionText: The word UNIONISED is a heteronym in some dialects. What are its two meanings?
options: A) UN-ion-ised (formed a labour union) OR un-ION-ised (not converted to ions)
B) Both mean related to trade unions
C) Both mean chemical processes
D) The meanings are identical in all contexts
explanation: UNIONISED can mean: 1) having formed or joined a trade union (with stress on UNION); 2) not having been ionised (with stress on ION, un-ION-ised). The two readings depend on whether UN- means not, or UNION is the root.

questionText: Which sentence uses COMPACT as a verb (com-PACT)?
options: A) The machine compacts the waste into small cubes.
B) She kept a compact in her handbag.
C) The nations signed a compact to reduce emissions.
D) He reached a compact with his business partners.
explanation: COMPACT as a verb (com-PACT) means to compress or pack tightly together. As a noun (COM-pact) it means a small cosmetic case or a formal agreement; as an adjective it means closely and neatly packed.

questionText: The word AUGUST is a heteronym. What are its two meanings?
options: A) AW-gust (the eighth month) OR aw-GUST (respected and impressive)
B) Both refer to the summer month
C) Both mean impressive in different contexts
D) AW-gust means impressive and aw-GUST is the month
explanation: AUGUST /ˈɔːɡəst/ (capitalised) is the eighth month of the year. August /ɔːˈɡʌst/ (lowercase, adjective) means respected and impressive. They are technically capitonyms with slightly different stress.

questionText: Which sentence uses MODERATE as an adjective (MOD-er-ate)?
options: A) She holds moderate political views, avoiding extremes.
B) The panel chose her to moderate the debate.
C) He was asked to moderate the online discussion forum.
D) It is important to moderate the tone of the conversation.
explanation: MODERATE as an adjective (MOD-er-ate) means average in amount, not extreme, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (mod-er-ATE) meaning to preside over or make less extreme, it stresses the third syllable.

questionText: The word NUMBER is a subtle heteronym. What makes it interesting?
options: A) It means a numerical figure, but also means more numb (comparative of numb)
B) It refers only to mathematics in all uses
C) It means both a song and a mathematical value
D) Number has only one meaning and pronunciation
explanation: NUMBER is a subtle heteronym: /ˈnʌmbər/ means a numeral or quantity; /ˈnʌmər/ is the comparative of NUMB (more numb). My fingers are NUMBER (more numb) than before is a valid but unusual use.

questionText: Which sentence uses INTIMATE as a verb (in-ti-MATE)?
options: A) She intimated that changes were coming without stating them outright.
B) They are intimate friends who have known each other for decades.
C) He shared his most intimate thoughts in the diary.
D) The two countries maintained intimate diplomatic relations.
explanation: INTIMATE as a verb (in-ti-MATE) means to hint or suggest something indirectly, stressed on the third syllable. As an adjective (IN-ti-mate) it means closely personal or private, stressed on the first syllable.

questionText: The word APPROPRIATE is a heteronym. Which sentence uses it as a verb?
options: A) The committee appropriated funds for the new project.
B) It is not appropriate to use mobile phones during the meeting.
C) Her appropriate response impressed the interviewers.
D) He chose an appropriate gift for the occasion.
explanation: APPROPRIATE as a verb (ap-pro-pri-ATE) means to take something for one own use, stressed on the fourth syllable. As an adjective (ap-PRO-pri-ate) meaning suitable, it stresses the second syllable.

questionText: Which sentence uses CLOSE as an adverb meaning near?
options: A) She stood close beside him throughout the ceremony.
B) Please close the window before leaving the room.
C) The close vote was decided by a single margin.
D) She was asked to close the meeting with a summary.
explanation: CLOSE /kloʊs/ as an adjective or adverb means near or nearby. CLOSE /kloʊz/ as a verb means to shut. She stood CLOSE beside him uses the /kloʊs/ (near) pronunciation as an adverb.

questionText: The word DIFFUSE is a heteronym. What are its two uses?
options: A) dif-FUSE (verb: to spread) OR DIF-fuse (adjective: spread over a large area)
B) Both mean to defuse a bomb
C) Both are pronounced identically
D) dif-FUSE means an adjective and DIF-fuse means a verb
explanation: DIFFUSE as a verb means to spread or disperse something. As an adjective meaning spread over a large area or not clear and concise, the stress pattern may shift slightly. Both are pronounced /dɪˈfjuːz/ for the verb and /ˈdɪfjuːs/ for the adjective.

questionText: Which sentence uses CONSOLE as a noun (CON-sole)?
options: A) She sat at the game console for hours.
B) He tried to console her after the devastating loss.
C) The therapist consoled the grieving family.
D) Nothing could console him after the news.
explanation: CONSOLE as a noun (CON-sole) means a panel of controls or a gaming device, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (con-SOLE) meaning to comfort, it is stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: The word RECORD is the most classic stress-shift heteronym. What is the rule?
options: A) Nouns are stressed on the first syllable (RE-cord); verbs on the second (re-CORD)
B) Verbs are stressed on the first syllable; nouns on the second
C) Both are always stressed on the first syllable
D) Stress does not change between noun and verb
explanation: The general rule for two-syllable noun-verb pairs: NOUNS are stressed on the FIRST syllable (RE-cord, PRO-test, OB-ject), and VERBS are stressed on the SECOND syllable (re-CORD, pro-TEST, ob-JECT). This applies to many English pairs.

questionText: Which sentence uses TRANSFER as a noun (TRANS-fer)?
options: A) She requested a transfer to the London office.
B) Please transfer the funds to the new account.
C) He will transfer to a different team next month.
D) The bank will transfer the money automatically.
explanation: TRANSFER as a noun (TRANS-fer) means the act of moving from one place to another, stressed on the first syllable. As a verb (trans-FER) it means to move something, stressed on the second syllable.

questionText: How does the stress pattern change in TORMENT (noun vs verb)?
options: A) Noun: TOR-ment (first syllable); Verb: tor-MENT (second syllable)
B) Noun: tor-MENT (second syllable); Verb: TOR-ment (first syllable)
C) Both noun and verb stress the first syllable
D) Both noun and verb stress the second syllable
explanation: TORMENT follows the classic noun-verb stress-shift pattern: the noun TOR-ment means great suffering, while the verb tor-MENT means to cause suffering. The noun stresses the first syllable; the verb stresses the second.

questionText: Which sentence uses REFUND as a verb (re-FUND)?
options: A) She asked the shop for a refund.
B) The store will refund your money within seven days.
C) He received a full refund after returning the item.
D) The refund arrived in the mail yesterday.
explanation: REFUND as a verb (re-FUND, stressed on the second syllable) means to return money. As a noun (RE-fund, stressed on the first syllable) it refers to the money returned. Option B uses it as a verb.

questionText: In the word ESSAY, how does pronunciation differ between noun and verb uses?
options: A) Noun: ES-say; Verb: es-SAY
B) Noun: es-SAY; Verb: ES-say
C) Both uses are pronounced identically
D) The verb form adds a final -ing sound
explanation: ESSAY as a noun (ES-say) refers to a piece of writing; as a verb (es-SAY) it means to attempt or try. This archaic verbal use of essay follows the noun-verb stress-shift pattern common in English.

questionText: Which option correctly identifies IMPORT used as a noun?
options: A) Many countries import oil from the Middle East.
B) The import of luxury goods increased this year.
C) Businesses that import raw materials face tariffs.
D) The government plans to import more technology.
explanation: In option B, IMPORT is used as a noun (IM-port), referring to goods brought into a country. In options A, C, and D, import is used as a verb (im-PORT), meaning to bring goods from another country.

questionText: Which sentence uses INSULT as a noun (IN-sult)?
options: A) He would never insult a colleague deliberately.
B) Do not insult the teacher with such behaviour.
C) The remark was a grave insult to her intelligence.
D) She did not mean to insult anyone with her comment.
explanation: In option C, INSULT is used as a noun (IN-sult, first syllable stressed), meaning an offensive remark. In the other options it is used as a verb (in-SULT, second syllable stressed), meaning to speak offensively to someone.

questionText: The word EXPORT can function as both noun and verb. Which sentence uses it as a verb (ex-PORT)?
options: A) Coffee is a major export of Brazil.
B) The company will export its products to Asia.
C) Oil is the countrys biggest export.
D) The export of weapons is strictly controlled.
explanation: In option B, EXPORT is used as a verb (ex-PORT, stress on second syllable), meaning to send goods to another country. In options A, C, and D it functions as a noun (EX-port, stress on first syllable) referring to goods sold abroad.
